title: Weather Almanac
intro: A field guide to the weather: what's coming, what it does, and how to make the most of it. Keep it handy.

entries.title: Welcome
pages:
The weather in this world changes all the time: rain and storms, fog and heatwaves, blizzards and sandstorms. It's different in cold, temperate and arid places, and it changes with the seasons.

This almanac explains all of it. Pick a chapter from the contents; scroll or use the arrows to turn pages.

pages.text: Use a barometer for a weather report: the weather here, the wind, the season, the local climate, the tide on the coast, the forecast and any storm on its way. While you hold it, a forecast panel shows in the corner of the screen.
Hold a thermometer to see the air temperature and how warm you feel. Use it for a full reading.

entries.title: The Weather Radio

pages.text: Keep a weather radio in your inventory and it warns you when severe storms are closing in, when a tornado is near, when dangerous weather is coming up, in extreme cold or heat, and about blood moons, meteor showers and geomagnetic storms.

pages: Use it to switch it on or off. Sneak and use it for a bulletin: the weather, the forecast and the nearest storm.

pages.text: The handheld radar and the weather radar block open a radar scope. It shows storm cells colour-coded by type, which way they're heading, when they'll reach you, and any tornadoes. Scroll to zoom out to 3,200 blocks.
The weather radar block also gives off a comparator signal: the closer the nearest storm, the stronger it is.

entries.title: Climates
pages:
Every weather plays out differently in cold, temperate and arid climates. A thunderstorm is a dry dust storm in the desert; a hurricane is a whiteout in the tundra.

The forecast leans toward weather that suits where players actually are, so deserts get more sandstorms and the north more snow.

entries.title: Clear, Overcast and Fog
pages:
Clear: blue skies. After rain a rainbow appears opposite the sun, and some clear nights in the cold bring auroras.

Overcast: grey skies hide the sun and stars, and the world gets a little darker.

Fog: about 24 blocks of visibility; a dusty haze in deserts. In freezing air, fog leaves everything white with hoarfrost.

entries.title: Rain
pages:
Drizzle is light and gentle. Rain makes crops open to the sky grow faster and leaves puddles on flat ground. Heavy rain is a downpour with misty visibility and wind (heavy snow in the cold).

After rain, leaves keep dripping for a while, frogs start croaking and worms come up.

entries.title: Thunderstorms
pages: Rain, thunder and lightning with gusty wind. Thunder arrives after the flash: the further away the strike, the longer the wait. Thunderstorms can spawn waterspouts over open water.

entries.title: Supercells
pages: A severe storm under a green-tinted sky: hail, constant lightning and tornadoes. Get underground.

entries.title: Hurricanes
pages: Hurricanes form out over warm sea and come in toward the coast on a track that curves round as they go. Warm water feeds them: watch the radio for the category climbing. Over land, or cold water, they weaken, and in the end all that's left is a big rainstorm.

Hurricane-force wind shoves players, mobs and items around, with torrential rain and flying leaves; the sea surges up onto low coasts and branches come down. Spiral bands of rain sweep round with lulls between them.

In the middle of a strong one there's a calm, clear eye. Don't be fooled: the other side of the eyewall is on its way.

entries.title: Derechos
pages: A derecho is a long line of violent thunderstorms racing across the land, several times faster than any other storm. On the radar it shows as a long orange band. The wind is ferocious and breaks branches off trees, so expect clearing up to do afterwards. They come in summer.

entries.title: Hail, Sleet and Ice
pages:
Hail hurts anything caught outside (a helmet or umbrella protects you) and can knock crops back.

Sleet is icy, slanting rain that chills and slows you, and glazes still water with thin ice.

An ice storm coats the ground and treetops in slippery glaze that melts once it's over.

entries.title: Snow and Blizzards
pages: Snow falls in cold places (cold rain elsewhere). A blizzard is a whiteout with driving snow and drifts up to 4 layers deep. Out in a blizzard you freeze; dress warmly or find a fire.

entries.title: Gales, Sand and Heat
pages:
A gale blows leaves around, pushes everything and makes arrows drift.

A sandstorm is a wall of sand under an orange sky (storm goggles let you see through it).

A heatwave brings a hazy amber sky; standing in the sun costs extra hunger and crops grow slower. Hot nights flicker with silent heat lightning.

entries.title: Seasons
pages:
Spring, summer, autumn and winter each last 7 days by default, and each reshapes the forecast: spring storms, summer heatwaves, hurricanes and derechos, autumn fog and gales, winter blizzards and ice storms.

Temperate plains get snow in winter, and it melts again in spring.

Leaves turn gold, orange and red through autumn and drift down, piling up under the trees. Winter dulls the grass; spring greens it up again, with blossom petals drifting from the trees.

If Serene Seasons is installed, its calendar is used instead.

entries.title: Storm Cells
pages: Besides the world-wide weather, storm cells form on the horizon and drift across the map with the wind, so players far apart can have different weather. Watch for the low, dark cloud deck with shafts of rain hanging under it.

entries.title: Local Climates
pages:
The land shapes the weather. Valleys are calmer and fill with fog at dawn. Peaks are windier. Land downwind of a mountain range lies in its rain shadow and gets less rain. In the cold, big lakes bring lake-effect snow to the land downwind, even on calm days.

The barometer and the F3 screen tell you the local climate.

entries.title: The Monsoon
pages: Summer is the rainy season in jungles and savannas. Savannas, which normally never see rain, get it then. Rice loves it.

entries.title: Floods and Storm Surges
pages: In heavy storms low water can spill over its banks (flash floods are off by default). Hurricanes push the sea up onto low beaches. In the first days of spring, melting snow swells the rivers. The water always goes down again afterwards.

pages.text: Sandbags hold the water back: no flood water appears within 2 blocks of one.

entries.title: Tides
pages: The sea rises and falls twice a day, highest around noon and midnight. Tides are strongest around full and new moons (spring tides) and weakest at the half moons. The highest spring tides wash over low beaches for a while. The barometer tells you the tide when you're near the coast.

entries.title: Rough Seas
pages: Storms make open water rough: whitecaps and spray, and boats get shoved by the wind and tossed by the swell. Keep a firm hand on the oars.

entries.title: Frozen Rivers and Thin Ice
pages:
In winter and in the cold, ponds and rivers freeze over from the banks.

Ice over open water is thin unless it's bitterly cold. It cracks under you if you sprint across it or stand around on it, and eventually gives way. Crouch to spread your weight.

entries.title: Rainbows and Auroras
pages: A rainbow appears opposite the sun when rain clears up during the day. On some clear nights, auroras shimmer over the northern sky in cold places.

entries.title: Halos, Sun Dogs and Sunbeams
pages:
On icy days and under thin, high cloud, a ring of light circles the sun (or the moon) at a fixed distance. When the sun is low, two bright spots called sun dogs sit level with it, one on each side.

When the sun shines through broken cloud or morning mist, sunbeams fan out across the sky.

entries.title: Shooting Stars and Meteors
pages: Shooting stars streak across clear night skies. About one night in seven brings a meteor shower with dozens of them, and now and then a meteor comes down, leaving a meteorite. Mine it for raw iron, gold nuggets and sometimes a diamond (silk touch keeps the block).

entries.title: Geomagnetic Storms
pages: On some aurora nights a geomagnetic storm hits: auroras reach south into temperate lands, compasses spin and radar screens fill with static.

entries.title: Blood Moons
pages: Some full moons rise blood red. Monsters swarm in the dark under them, and nobody can sleep the night away. Light up your base, shut the door, and wait for dawn.

entries.title: Air and Body Temperature
pages:
Every spot has an air temperature: the biome, the season, the height, the time of day and the weather all play a part. How warm you feel also depends on your clothes, on being in water, and on heat nearby: campfires, fires, lava, lit furnaces, even torches. Buildings and caves even things out.

Your body temperature follows slowly: you cool down over half a minute or so out in the cold, and warm up quickly by a fire.

Below 0 °C frost creeps in. In deadly cold you start to freeze and slowly take damage.

Above 32 °C the heat makes you hungry; above 48 °C you get heatstroke unless you cool off in water or rain.

pages.text: A winter coat (or leather armour) keeps you warm. A tent is a warm, sheltered place to sleep.
Hot cocoa gives Warmth for 3 minutes, and a winter stew for a minute and a half.
A tent is a portable shelter: milder inside, safe from the weather. Sleeping in it skips the night but never sets your spawn point.
A sun hat shades you from the midday sun.
A melon cooler (or cooked icefish) gives Refreshed, cooling you down. Shade, water and rain help too, and a winter coat in a heatwave is a bad idea.

entries.title: Rain and Crops
pages: Crops open to the sky grow faster in the rain, slower in heatwaves and in winter. Hail can knock them back. In a drought, crops on dry farmland wilt.

entries.title: Frost and Greenhouses
pages:
On freezing nights, frost damages crops out in the open and knocks them back a few stages; seedlings can die.

A crop with glass or glass panes above it is in a greenhouse: safe from frost and hail, and still growing in winter (though it misses out on the rain).

pages.text: Rice turns up in the grass of jungles, savannas and swamps. Plant it on farmland. It races ahead in the rain and the monsoon, keeps going next to water, and stalls in dry weather.
Three handfuls make a filling bowl of rice.

Kale turns up in the grass of cold places. It's a hardy winter green: frost doesn't hurt it, it keeps growing through the winter and it even likes the cold, but it slows right down in the heat. Eat it raw, or in a winter stew.
In autumn, leaves pile up under the trees, and storms bring more down. You can wade through them, and a deep pile softens a fall. They rot away over the winter.
A rake gathers up the leaf piles (and fallen branches) in a 5x5 area. Compost the leaves, or put them back where you like.

entries.title: Food in the Heat
pages: Raw meat and fish go off in hot weather, a piece at a time, in your inventory and in chests. Carrying ice keeps your own food fresh.

pages.text: An icebox never lets food spoil. Neither does a chest or barrel with ice, packed ice, blue ice or snow next to it: build an ice house.
The ice saw cuts whole blocks of ice out of frozen lakes, ready to pack around your food.

entries.title: Fishing in the Weather
pages: Fish bite better in the rain: you sometimes pull up a second one.

pages.text: Fish out in the open during a thunderstorm, supercell, hurricane or derecho and you might catch a stormfish. Cooked, it gives a burst of Haste.
Fish through a hole in the ice, in winter or in the cold, to catch icefish. Cooked, they cool you down.

Worms come up onto the grass after rain. Dig grass or dirt while it's wet for a good chance of finding some. Hold them in your off hand when you cast: a baited hook gets bites sooner, and better ones.

entries.title: Droughts and Wildfires
pages: During heatwaves, dry grass in deserts and savannas can catch fire, crops on unwatered farmland wilt and cauldrons in the sun dry up (sometimes leaving salt behind).

pages.text: Icicles grow under roof edges and can fall on whoever is below. Blizzards set off avalanches on steep slopes. Salt melts ice, snow and icicles around where you use it.

entries.title: Lightning
pages: Lightning fuses sand into glass. Big storms sometimes bring ball lightning, which drifts around and zaps anything that gets too close. Lightning that strikes where it isn't raining can start fires, and summer heatwaves bring the odd dry strike.

entries.title: Charging Tools
pages: Leave a tool or weapon lying on an anvil or a copper block in a thunderstorm (a lightning rod nearby helps). If lightning strikes it, it's charged for five minutes: it mines faster and hits harder, with a crackle of sparks.

entries.title: Storm Debris
pages: Derechos, hurricanes and supercells break branches off trees and strip their leaves. Clear the branches for sticks, or leave them to rot away after a few days.

pages.text: Blocks hail. Hold it while falling to drift down slowly with no fall damage.
See much further in sandstorms and blizzards.

entries.title: Paraglider

pages.text: Hold use while falling to open it. Glide where you look: look down to dive, up to slow down.

pages: The wind carries you along. Warm air rising off lava, fires, campfires, sun-baked sand on hot days and windy ridges lifts you up, so you can ride thermals for miles. No fall damage while you glide, but it wears out over time.

pages.text: Gives off a redstone signal. Use it to switch between precipitation, storm danger, wind, a weather code and the season. A villager who claims one becomes a meteorologist.
Wails and powers redstone while a tornado or waterspout is within 160 blocks.
Fills with rainwater. Empty it with a bucket when it's full, or with bottles.
The weather vane points into the wind; comparators read the direction.
The windmill turns into the wind and gives off redstone as strong as the wind. It works best high up in the open.
A wall board that shows the current weather, the season and the next three weathers.
Put it under a lightning rod to store up to 4 strikes. A redstone pulse from the side, back or bottom lets one out as a strong pulse from the front. Comparators read the charge.
Leave it in a tornado's path. Probes near a tornado record readings and drop storm data when broken (more from close to the funnel). Meteorologists buy storm data.
Fire a cloud seeding rocket straight up and it seeds a rain cloud (sometimes a thunderstorm) overhead.

entries.title: The Weather Altar

pages.text: End-game weather control. Offer it an item to call up a weather; it needs a few minutes to recover between uses.

pages: Sunflower: clear. Water bucket: rain. Lightning rod: thunderstorm. Snow block: snow. Packed ice: blizzard. Ice: ice storm. Blaze powder: heatwave. Feather: gale. Sand: sandstorm. Cobweb: fog. Ghast tear: supercell. Heart of the sea: hurricane. Breeze rod: derecho.

entries.title: Weather and Mobs
pages:
Strays come out in blizzards and snow, husks in desert sandstorms and heatwaves, and drowned near water in heavy rain and hurricanes. Polar bears wander in out of blizzards.

Animals look for shelter in rough weather, sheep grow a thicker coat in winter (more wool), and villagers go indoors during storms.

entries.title: The Meteorologist
pages: A villager who claims a weather station becomes a meteorologist. They buy paper, copper and storm data, and sell weather gear, from thermometers and umbrellas up to lightning batteries and weather radars.

entries.title: Wildlife
pages: Birds sing on spring and summer days, crickets chirp on summer nights and frogs croak after rain. Fireflies glow over the grass on warm summer evenings, and in spring and autumn flocks of geese fly over in a V.

entries.title: Nether Weather
pages: Choking ash storms, harmless glowing ember falls, and fire rain that sets exposed creatures and flammable blocks alight.

entries.title: End Weather
pages: Violet void storms, with gusts every few seconds that push you toward the edge of the island.

entries.title: Finding Volcanoes
pages:
Now and then a volcano rises out of the land: a great cone of basalt, tuff and blackstone with a crater at the top and a lake of lava inside. Out at sea they make volcanic islands.

Old lava flows streak the flanks, and steam vents hiss on the upper slopes, crusted with yellow sulfur.

A barometer or weather radio names the nearest volcano you know of, how far away it is and what it's doing. Volcanoes show up on the weather radar as small triangles.

Volcanoes never form on top of villages.

entries.title: Eruptions
pages:
A volcano sleeps for days at a time (only while someone is nearby). When it wakes, the ground rumbles and shakes for a few minutes and smoke rises from the crater: that's your warning.

Then it erupts: lava fountains, a towering column of ash, lightning in the plume and blasts you'll hear long after you see them.

Lava bombs arc out of the crater and burst where they land, setting things alight. Lava pours over the rim and creeps down the slopes.

Afterwards the volcano cools: the spilled lava crusts over into basalt (with some magma and the odd bit of obsidian), and it goes back to sleep.

entries.title: Ash Fall
pages:
An eruption's ash cloud drifts downwind for a long way. Under it the sky goes dark, grey ash drifts down and piles up on the ground, crops struggle without the sun, and breathing it in leaves you weak, unless you wear something on your head.

Rain washes the ash back into the soil.

entries.title: Volcanic Finds
pages:
Volcanic ash is a fine fertilizer: use it on a crop as you would bone meal. Two ash make a bone meal.

Mine sulfur crust for sulfur, and grind it with charcoal and bone meal into gunpowder.

Steam vents are warm to stand near, but scald you if you walk on them; sneak across. Silk Touch picks one up.

entries.title: Seismograph
pages:
A seismograph feels a volcano waking up before you can. It gives a redstone signal while a volcano within 1024 blocks rumbles, getting stronger as the eruption nears and the closer you are, up to 15 during an eruption.

Wire it to a bell, a lamp or a door as an early warning.

entries.title: Weather Fronts
pages:
A cold front is a long line of storms racing across the map: a squall of wind, downpours and thunder. Behind it the air is about 7 degrees colder and the wind swings round.

A warm front is a wide, slow band of low cloud and drizzle, with milder air behind it. Both are most common in spring and autumn.

entries.title: Afternoon Storms
pages:
On summer days (and any day in the tropics) the sun heats the ground and the clouds start to tower up around midday. Watch them: by the afternoon some of them grow into thunderstorms, even hailstorms, and they die away again by dusk.

Thunderstorms anywhere tower into tall, anvil-topped clouds you can see from far away.

entries.title: Sea Fog
pages: On cool, calm mornings a bank of fog builds up out at sea and rolls in over the coast, thick and white. It burns off by the middle of the morning.

entries.title: Wildfire Smoke
pages: Fires burning out in the open send up tall columns of smoke. A big wildfire sends a pall of smoke drifting downwind: an orange-brown haze that turns the sun into a dull red ball.

entries.title: St. Elmo's Fire
pages:
In a thunderstorm, blue sparks crackle on lightning rods and on metal tools you hold up.

If sparks start dancing around you and your hair stands on end, lightning is about to strike right there: you have a few seconds to get away.

entries.title: Hail and Glass
pages: Big hail cracks or smashes glass that's open to the sky, and a cracked pane goes on the next hit. Greenhouse roofs take a beating in a hailstorm. Tinted glass is tough enough to hold, or put a proper roof over your glass.

entries.title: Mudslides
pages: After a couple of minutes of pouring rain, waterlogged soil on steep slopes can give way and slide downhill as mud, taking the grass and flowers with it. Don't build at the foot of a bare, steep hill.

entries.title: Diamond Dust
pages: On bitterly cold, clear, still mornings the air fills with glittering ice crystals, and a pillar of light stands straight up from the low sun.

entries.title: Volcanic Smog
pages: As an eruption dies down, the volcano leaves a yellowish smog drifting downwind with an acid drizzle. Copper turns green faster, leaves wither and fall, crops struggle, and the rain stings bare skin: wear a helmet.

entries.title: Hot Springs
pages:
Hot springs are patches of white sinter with steaming pools ringed in orange and yellow, bubbling mud and hissing vents. The pools are warm: soak in one to warm up and slowly heal.

Geysers sit on little mounds and erupt every few minutes, throwing anything above them high into the air. Glide over one with a paraglider for a huge lift.

entries.title: Crater Lakes
pages: A crater lake is a long-extinct volcano: a grassy, wooded cone with a deep, cold lake filling its crater.

entries.title: Lava Tubes
pages:
Under the flanks of active volcanoes run lava tubes, caves left behind when old lava flows crusted over while the lava inside drained away. Look for skylights where the roof has fallen in.

Volcanic islands have black sand beaches. Black sand smelts into glass.

entries.title: Meteor Craters
pages: Old impact craters are round bowls with a raised rim, grassed over by now, sometimes with a pond in the bottom. Dig down in the middle: the meteorite itself is buried a few blocks under the floor.

entries.title: Salt Flats
pages:
Salt flats are dead-flat dry lake beds in the desert, crusted white. Mine the crust for salt.

When a storm passes over, the flat floods into a shallow lake that mirrors the sky, then dries back out to salt. On hot days a mirage shimmers across the flats like water you can never reach.

entries.title: Glaciers
pages:
Glaciers flow down cold mountainsides: packed ice with veins of blue ice, snowy higher up and bare lower down. Crevasses cut across them, and many hide under a thin bridge of powder snow. Watch your step.

In summer the lower end melts back a little and meltwater runs off it.

Some glaciers have an ice cave running into their foot, its walls glowing blue.

Where a glacier reaches the sea, great slabs break off its front now and then and float away as icebergs.
Where a glacier steepens it breaks up into an icefall of tottering seracs and crevasses. In summer, meltwater pours down moulins: shafts drilled straight down through the ice.

entries.title: Tidal Flats
pages: Tidal flats are wide stretches of mud at the edge of the sea, level with the water. High tide washes over them; at low tide they're bare, dotted with tide pools of seagrass and sea pickles. Brush the sand at the bottom of a tide pool for buried treasure.

entries.title: Dune Fields
pages: Dune fields are rows of tall sand dunes across the prevailing wind, each with a long, gentle slope and a steep face. In sandstorms the wind carries sand off the crests and drops it beyond, so the dunes slowly creep downwind.

Not all dune fields are alike: some are rows of dunes across the wind, some are scattered crescent barchans with their horns pointing downwind, some are long knife-edged seif ridges running with the wind, and some are great star dunes with arms reaching out every way.

entries.title: Droughts
pages:
After a dry spell, mostly in summer, the weather can turn against rain for days on end. The grass browns, crops on dry farmland wilt, and wildfires catch far more easily.

Shallow ponds dry up, leaving cracked mud. When the drought finally breaks, with a storm, the rain fills them up again. Water next to farmland is left alone.

entries.title: Cold Snaps
pages: Now and then, mostly in winter, bitterly cold, clear, still air settles in for a day or two. Lakes and rivers freeze over from the shore inward, even where they usually don't. Crops get frosted, animals huddle under cover, and everything turns white with frost overnight. It all thaws again afterwards.

entries.title: Föhn Winds
pages: When a strong wind blows over a mountain range, it drops its rain on the far side and warms up as it comes down again. On the sheltered side it arrives warm and bone-dry (a föhn, or chinook), and the snow melts away astonishingly fast.

entries.title: Frost Hollows
pages: On clear, calm nights cold air slides downhill and pools in valley bottoms, which get several degrees colder than the slopes above. Frost comes earlier and harder in a hollow: don't plant tender crops there.

entries.title: Steam Fog
pages: When the air is far colder than the water, unfrozen lakes and rivers steam on still mornings, wisps of fog rising off the water like smoke.

entries.title: Ice Breakup
pages:
In the spring thaw, river ice breaks up into floes that drift away downstream. You can ride one, like a boat. Where floes pile up against each other in a narrow stretch, an ice jam forms, and the river backs up and floods its banks until the jam melts.

In the cold seas, sea ice breaks up into floes in spring, and icebergs drift by out in open water. You can ride a berg too.

entries.title: Dust Carried Far
pages: A big sandstorm lifts dust high enough for the wind to carry it far beyond the desert: a tawny haze that dims the sun. It settles on the snow, turning it pink, leaves a film of dust on rooftops and rock, and rain falling through it comes down reddish-brown.

entries.title: Rare Sights
pages: On a dark night, watch distant thunderstorms: now and then a red sprite flickers high above the cloud tops. On some summer nights, noctilucent clouds glow electric blue low in the north long after sunset.

A squall line comes in under a shelf cloud, a long, low, dark wedge. Under the anvil of a big storm hang pouches of mammatus. After night rain under a full moon, look for a pale moonbow, and when a low sun shines through thin fog, a broad white fogbow.

entries.title: Arroyos
pages: Dry, sandy riverbeds winding across deserts and badlands. They're bone-dry almost all the time, but when a real storm breaks over one, a flash flood comes racing down the channel. Don't camp in a wash.

entries.title: Cenotes and Sinkholes
pages:
A cenote is a sinkhole in the jungle where a cave roof fell in long ago: a sheer-sided shaft with deep, clear water at the bottom, hung with vines and stalactites.

After a long downpour, the ground over a cave close under the surface can give way into a brand-new sinkhole.

entries.title: Oases
pages: Where water comes up in a hollow among the dunes: a pool ringed with grass, reeds and palm trees. The palms have cocoa, a welcome find in the desert.

entries.title: Waterfalls
pages: Streams pouring off cliffs into a deep plunge pool they've dug out at the foot. Spray billows up from the pool, and with the sun at your back there's a rainbow in it.

entries.title: Basalt Columns
pages: An old lava flow that cracked into columns as it cooled, worn by the sea into a pavement of polygonal stepping stones running down into the water.

entries.title: Sea Stacks and Arches
pages: Pillars of layered rock standing off a rocky coast, notched at the waterline by the waves and capped with a scrap of turf. One is still an arch, with the sea running through it.

entries.title: Atolls
pages: In warm seas: a ring of coral reef round a shallow, sandy lagoon, with low islets and palms here and there along it. Outside the reef, the bottom drops away into the deep.

entries.title: Fjords
pages: Long, deep arms of the sea reaching into cold mountains, cut by glaciers long ago. Sheer rock walls drop straight into deep water, with a shallow sill across the mouth.

entries.title: Erratics and Moraines
pages: What the ice sheets left behind: long, curving ridges of rubble (moraines), and great boulders of rock that doesn't belong anywhere near here, carried for miles on the ice. Glaciers have a moraine round their foot too.

entries.title: Peat Bogs
pages:
Wet, mossy flats over deep peat, dotted with dark pools, cotton grass and cranberries. Dig the peat and burn it in a furnace.

Lightning can set a bog smouldering. A peat fire creeps slowly underground for a long time, sending up smoke, and stepping on it burns. Water puts it out.

entries.title: Rockfall
pages: On mild days in spring, and whenever it thaws, water that froze in the cracks overnight lets go: rocks break off cliffs and tumble down, piling up as scree at the bottom. Don't linger under a cliff in the thaw.

entries.title: Breezes
pages: On a calm, sunny day the land warms faster than the sea, so a cool sea breeze blows in off the water in the afternoon; at night it turns round into a gentle land breeze. In the mountains, valley winds blow uphill by day, and at night cold mountain winds slide back down, strongest off snow and ice.

entries.title: Microbursts and Heat Bursts
pages:
A thunderstorm can drop a microburst: a column of cold air slamming into the ground and blasting outward, flattening crops and stripping leaves in a circle. It's over in a minute.

At night, a dying storm sometimes collapses into a heat burst instead: a sudden gale of hot, bone-dry air.

entries.title: Haboobs
pages: In the desert, the cold outflow from a thunderstorm picks up the dust and drives it ahead in a towering wall that swallows the sun. Inside it's dark, orange and roaring. Get under cover and wait for it to pass.

entries.title: Fire Whirls and Fire Clouds
pages:
A big enough wildfire makes its own weather. The rising heat spins up fire whirls, whirling columns of flame that wander about spreading the fire.

Over the biggest fires a fire cloud builds: a dirty, smoke-stained thunderhead that throws dry lightning downwind, starting new fires.

entries.title: Atmospheric Rivers
pages: Now and then, mostly in autumn and winter, a long, narrow river of moist air from the tropics comes ashore and stalls, soaking the coast with days of heavy rain (or heavy snow up in the cold). Expect floods.

entries.title: Virga
pages: In dry country you'll often see grey streaks of rain hanging under the clouds that never reach the ground: it's drying up on the way down.

entries.title: Rime and Snow Rollers
pages:
In freezing fog, the droplets freeze where they touch, and rime builds up in white feathers on the windward side of everything, more of it higher up. It melts when it warms up.

A strong wind over wet, sticky snow can roll it up into snow rollers, leaving a bare track behind each one.

entries.title: Lake Ice
pages: Thick lake ice is noisy. As the temperature changes around dawn and dusk it booms, pings and sings with strange, swooping notes. In hard frosts it cracks and buckles up into pressure ridges across the lake.

entries.title: Valley Inversions
pages: On cold, still, clear mornings the coldest air sinks into the valleys, trapped under a lid of warmer air. Smoke and haze pool under the lid in a flat-topped layer; climb above it and you look down on it.

entries.title: Fertile Floods
pages: Flood water leaves a layer of silt behind when it drains away. Crops on ground that was flooded grow faster for a few days.

entries.title: Earthquakes and Tsunamis
pages:
These are switched off unless you turn them on in the settings.

Earthquakes shake the ground, bring rocks down off cliffs and break the odd pane of glass.

A big quake under the sea sends a tsunami toward the nearest coast. The warning sign: the sea drawing back from the shore. A minute or two later the water comes surging in far over the beach. Run for high ground.

entries.title: The Coast
pages:
Storm waves slowly wear back natural cliffs, cutting a notch at the foot until the rock above comes down, and drag sand off beaches to drop it again as a bar just offshore. They never touch anything you've built.

On warm coasts at night, the breaking waves glow blue, and so does the water swirling round you as you swim.

entries.title: Double Rainbows
pages: Look outside a bright rainbow for a fainter second bow, with its colours the other way round. The sky between the two is darker than the sky around them: Alexander's dark band.

entries.title: Glories
pages: Stand on a mountain above a sea of fog with the sun low behind you, and your shadow falls on the fog, huge and ghostly (a Brocken spectre), with a little round rainbow, a glory, ringed round its head.

entries.title: Lenticular Clouds
pages: When a strong wind blows over mountains, smooth, lens-shaped clouds can sit perfectly still above and downwind of the peaks, like stacks of saucers.

entries.title: Twilight
pages:
Just after sunset (or before sunrise) look the other way: a dark blue band low on the horizon is the Earth's own shadow, with a pink glow above it, the Belt of Venus.

At the very moment the sun disappears into the sea on a clear evening, its last sliver can flash green.

entries.title: Light Pillars
pages: On bitterly cold, clear, still nights, tiny flat ice crystals hang in the air and catch the light of lanterns, torches and fires, standing columns of light up over them.

entries.title: Iridescent Clouds
pages: Thin cloud passing near the sun sometimes shimmers with pastel pinks and greens.

entries.title: Travertine Terraces
pages: Warm springs spilling down a hillside leave their minerals behind as the water cools, building white rims that hold a staircase of shallow, steaming blue pools.

entries.title: Tufa Lakes
pages: Salty lakes ringed with a crust of salt, with knobbly pale towers of tufa standing in the shallows where springs once bubbled up through the lake bed.

entries.title: Hoodoos and Arches
pages: In the badlands and deserts, rain and frost have worn the soft rock into hoodoos, tall banded spires each sheltered by a hard caprock, and natural arches with the sky showing through them.

entries.title: Slot Canyons
pages: Cracks in the sandstone barely wider than your shoulders but many times deeper, carved by flash floods into smooth, swirling walls of banded rock. Logs jammed high overhead show how deep the last flood ran. If it starts raining hard upstream, get out.

entries.title: Limestone Country
pages:
A limestone pavement is bare rock dissolved by the rain into flat slabs split by deep cracks, with ferns growing down in them.

In the jungle, the same rock has been dissolved away until only tower karst is left: sheer towers hung with vines, tufted with trees on top.

entries.title: Rivers
pages:
Oxbow lakes are the crescent-shaped loops of old river bends, cut off when the river took a short cut.

In cold, bare country, braided rivers weave across wide plains of gravel in a tangle of shallow channels.
Where a river meets the sea it builds a delta: a fan of low, muddy marsh split by channels, with raised banks along them and sand bars (and quicksand) at the front. The high tide creeps over it.

entries.title: Left by the Ice
pages:
Cirques are armchair-shaped hollows gouged into mountainsides by small glaciers, with a sheer headwall and a little lake, a tarn, in the floor.

Kettle lakes are deep, round ponds where buried blocks of ice melted out, among mounds of gravel called kames.
Drumlins are smooth, whale-backed hills all lying the same way, blunt where the ice came from. An esker, a long winding gravel ridge, is the bed of a river that ran in a tunnel under the ice.

entries.title: Permafrost
pages: Where the ground is frozen deep down all year, it cracks into a pattern of polygons with ice in the cracks. Pingos are hills with a core of solid ice, split open at the top, and thaw lakes sit where the ice has melted and the ground has slumped.

entries.title: Chalk Cliffs
pages:
Sheer white cliffs of chalk banded with dark flint, standing over a flat wave-cut platform, with sea caves in their foot.

Look for a blowhole on the clifftop: a hole at the top of a shaft from one of the caves. When a wave surges in it booms and blasts spray into the air, higher in rough seas and at high tide.

entries.title: Low Coasts
pages:
Barrier islands are long, thin islands of sand and dunes just off a low coast, with a shallow lagoon behind and an inlet the tide runs through.

Salt marshes are flat coastal meadows threaded with winding creeks. The bare mud of the low marsh floods at every high tide. Watch for quicksand.

entries.title: Little Volcanoes
pages:
Cinder cones are steep cones of black and red cinders with a crater on top, breached on one side where a lava flow broke out.

Maars are broad explosion craters sunk into flat ground, ringed with tuff and filled with a deep lake.

Mud volcanoes are little cones of grey mud with bubbling pools on top.

entries.title: Termite Mounds
pages: On the savanna, termites build tall towers of cemented earth over their nests, some low and domed, some steep spires taller than you are.

entries.title: Quicksand
pages: Sand so full of water it can't bear any weight: darker and glossier than the sand around it. You sink in to your waist and can barely move. Thrashing about doesn't help: sneak to work your way out slowly.

entries.title: New Weathers
pages:
Graupel: showers of soft, white snow pellets that bounce and roll, in chilly spring and autumn weather.

Thundersnow: a snowstorm heavy enough to throw lightning, the thunder muffled by the snow.

Freezing drizzle: fine drizzle falling through freezing air, glazing everything it touches.

entries.title: The Snowpack
pages: Over the winter, snowfall builds on snowfall into a deep snowpack, deepest high up, in the coldest places and among the trees. In spring it settles and melts away. Rain falling on deep snow melts it fast and the water runs straight into the rivers, which flood.

entries.title: Frozen Ground
pages: On frosty mornings, needle ice pushes up out of bare soil in crunchy columns, and can heave young crops right out of the farmland. Frost flowers grow on new ice in bitter, still cold. Both melt once the sun gets to them.

entries.title: Mountain Snow
pages:
Wind blowing snow over a ridge builds a cornice: a lip of snow overhanging the drop on the far side. Don't walk out on one: it can give way under you and set the slope below sliding.

On open snowfields, strong wind carves the snow into sharp ridges and furrows (sastrugi) lying across its path.

entries.title: Whirlwinds
pages:
Not every spinning column is a tornado from a supercell. Landspouts are thin, rope-like tornadoes that spin up under growing storms on the open plains. Gustnadoes are brief swirls of dust along a storm's gust front.

In bitter cold, steam devils twist up off unfrozen water, and on sunny, windy snowfields snow devils skitter about.

entries.title: Humid Heat
pages:
Humid air makes heat harder to bear, because sweat can't cool you down. On sticky days in the jungle or the swamp, or after rain, it feels a good deal hotter than the thermometer says.

On clear, calm, mild mornings, dew sparkles on the grass.

entries.title: Good Years and Bad
pages: The climate swings slowly between wet and dry spells a year or more long. A wet year brings more rain, storms and hurricanes and fewer droughts; a dry year, more heatwaves and droughts. Ask /rweather query which sort of year it is.

entries.title: Pollen
pages: On dry, breezy spring days, the woods give off clouds of yellow pollen that haze the air and settle in a film on still water.

entries.title: Rip Currents
pages: The water the surf piles up on a beach drains back out to sea in narrow, fast channels: rip currents. One will carry a swimmer straight out, faster than you can swim against it. Don't fight it: swim along the shore until you're out of it, then swim in.

entries.title: Waves and Foam
pages: A hurricane sends a long swell racing out ahead of it, so the sea gets rough even under a clear sky a long way from the storm. In a big sea, now and then a rogue wave far bigger than the rest comes out of nowhere and can capsize a boat. Storms whip up foam and throw it up the beach.
Beaches change with the seasons: winter storms drag the sand off, and calm summer swell carries it back up.

entries.title: Tidal Bores
pages: On the biggest tides, at full and new moon, the incoming tide can run up a river near the sea as a single breaking wave, roaring upstream against the current. Catch it in a boat and ride it.

entries.title: Whirlpools
pages: In some narrow straits, the tide racing through spins up a whirlpool between high and low water, strongest at spring tides. It drags boats and swimmers round and down. At slack water, around high and low tide, it's calm enough to cross.

entries.title: Algal Blooms and Pumice
pages:
In a long, hot, still summer, algae can bloom across the warm seas: the water turns murky rust-red, the fish die off or leave, and all your rod brings up is weed. A good storm breaks it up.

After a big undersea earthquake, rafts of floating pumice from an eruption on the sea bed drift across the sea.

entries.title: In the Sky
pages:
On dark, clear, moonless nights away from lights, the Milky Way arches right across the sky, and after dusk a faint cone of zodiacal light rises where the sun went down.

When sunbeams fan out from a low sun, look the other way: they converge again on the far horizon.

Thin ice cloud makes its own rainbows: a band of colour low under a high summer sun (the circumhorizontal arc, or fire rainbow), and an upside-down arc high over a low one (the circumzenithal arc). In polar winter twilight, nacreous clouds glow mother-of-pearl.

Look out for roll clouds rolling ahead of storms, rows of breaking-wave clouds, smooth caps over growing thunderheads, and round holes punched in high cloud. At night, spider lightning crawls along the underside of storm clouds.

And the old saying holds: red sky at night, fair weather tomorrow; red sky in the morning, rain on the way.

entries.title: Karst
pages: Tiankeng are giant sinkholes, sheer-walled and hundreds of feet deep, with a forest of their own on the floor. Blue holes are the same at sea: deep round shafts that show dark blue in the shallows.

Stone forests are fields of tall, sharp limestone pinnacles. Natural bridges arch over streams that cut beneath them, and some streams sink into a cave mouth altogether, coming out again at a spring further down.

entries.title: Volcanic
pages: A volcanic neck is the plug of an old volcano left standing as a tower of basalt columns when the rest wore away. Spatter cones line a fissure in a young lava field. Obsidian flows are thick, glassy tongues crusted with pumice. On the sea bed, lava that erupted underwater lies in mounds of rounded pillows.

entries.title: Ice and Cold
pages: Nunataks are rocky peaks poking up through an ice sheet. Rock glaciers are tongues of ice-cored rubble creeping down mountain valleys. Palsas are mounds of frozen peat in northern bogs. Stone circles form where frost sorts the stones from the soil, and on slopes they stretch into stripes. Penitentes are fields of tall snow spikes on high, dry peaks.

entries.title: Desert Rocks
pages: Yardangs are wind-carved ridges like upturned boats, all lying one way, on a pavement of stones. Inselbergs are huge isolated domes of rock. Mesas are flat-topped hills with banded cliffs, with buttes and spires nearby. Mushroom rocks balance wide caps on wind-worn stems.

On some dry lake beds, boulders sit at the end of long tracks, as though they'd sailed across. Fairy circles dot dry grassland in an even pattern. And after rain, the potholes (tinajas) in bare desert rock fill with water, until they dry out again.

entries.title: Mountains
pages: Horns are pyramidal peaks carved by glaciers on several sides, with knife-edge aretes between. Talus cones of scree pile up under cliffs, alluvial fans spread out of valleys onto the plain, and avalanche chutes are strips swept clear of trees down snowy slopes. Landslides leave bare scars in hillsides with a heap of debris below.

Hanging valleys end high on the wall of a glacial trough, their streams pouring off as waterfalls. Glacial lakes are turquoise with rock flour, dammed by moraines: in summer one may burst through and send a flood down the valley.

entries.title: Rivers
pages: River terraces are flat benches stepping up from a river, the floors of older, higher valleys. Rapids are rocky stretches with boulders in the stream and potholes worn into the bedrock. Gorges are deep, narrow, rock-walled valleys.

entries.title: Coasts
pages: Spits are long, curving fingers of sand growing out from the shore. Tombolos are sandbars tying an island to the mainland. Shingle beaches step up in storm ridges of pebbles. Raised beaches are old beaches left as flat terraces above today's shore. Rias are drowned river valleys winding inland as arms of the sea.

entries.title: Ancient Things
pages:
In the badlands, petrified forests are strewn with fallen logs turned to stone. Fossil beds show great bones weathering out of eroding banks: brush the gravel at their feet for finds.

In old forests, fallen trees become nurse logs, with saplings and fungi growing on them, beside the upturned root plates they pulled out of the ground.

entries.title: Settings
pages:
Open the settings from the Mods screen. The first page has one-click presets for the visual effects (Performance, Default, Cinematic) and a button for every setting.

Under Accessibility you can tone down lightning flashes and turn down screen effects like raindrops on the screen, heat shimmer and the roll of a boat at sea.

entries.title: Commands
pages:
/rweather query: the weather where you stand (and whether it's a wet or dry year).
/rweather forecast: the next three weathers.
/rweather storms: storm cells.
/rweather season: the season.
/rweather volcano: volcanoes nearby.
/rweather drought: any drought.

For operators: /rweather set, storm, next, tornado, meteor and drought start/end, and /rweather volcano create, wake, erupt and calm.
